processing: Black tea work on Menghai large-leaf material: withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried.
harvest_season: Not documented for this tea specifically; as with other Dian Hong, spring lots are generally prized.
appearance_dry: Plump strands with a dark sheen; tippy grades show golden-yellow down.
appearance_liquor: Typically a bright, deep red, as with other Dian Hong.
taste_profile: Rich aroma and a full, mellow body, in line with Dian Hong's reputation for strength and freshness.

brewing.notes: General large-leaf guidance: flash the first steeps, since long ones turn the strength rough.

vintage_note: Usually sold by harvest year and drunk within a year or two, as with other Dian Hong. Menghai is far better known for pu-erh, so check that a black tea label really states the year and category clearly.
description:
Menghai is famous for pu-erh, but this county in Xishuangbanna makes black tea too. Menghai Dian Hong is a Yunnan black tea from the local large-leaf plant.

The processing is ordinary black tea work. The leaf does the talking: stout strands and thick material, with tips usually described as golden yellow, where Fengqing's are chrysanthemum yellow.

In the cup it has a strong aroma and a mellow, thick body. Use short steeps, since this leaf turns brisk if you leave it. It also takes a Western mug well if you use less leaf.

Look for a clear statement of where the leaf is from, because Dian Hong is a broad label and Menghai is a name that sells. Compare it with a Fengqing Dian Hong to find out which end of Yunnan you prefer.
history: Menghai's place in Yunnan black tea goes back to September 1940, when the Fohai Experimental Tea Factory, forerunner of the Menghai Tea Factory, was set up. Fan Hejun made black and green samples from Menghai large-leaf leaf there. He is said to have rated the black tea above Keemun for colour and taste and above Indian tea for aroma, which is a maker's own judgement and not a neutral test.
